newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Brittan says WTO pact a breakthrough on labour.
newsitem.headline: Brittan says WTO pact a breakthrough on labour.

text.p: European Trade Commisisoner Sir Leon Brittan said on Friday the agreement between World Trade Organisation delegates meeting here this week was a breakthrough on global labour standards.
"I think that the agreements on labour standards does mark a breakthrough in the worldwide dialogue on this delicate but vital subject," Brittan told a news conference.

After days of intense negotiations at this week's inaugural World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial conference, a hard-fought compromise emerged late on Thursday that had just enough to enable North and South to proclaim victory.

Developing nations, led by India, Pakistan and Egypt, had refused to countenance any interference by the WTO in the area of workers' rights, fearing it would undermine their chief comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.

The United States and a string of European countries, by contrast, were equally insistent in clamouring for action to help 250 million child workers, mainly in the Third World, and to improve sweatshop conditions.

The final declaration satisfies poor countries because it firmly rejects the use of labour standards for protectionist purposes and says the International Labour Organisation, based like the WTO in Geneva, is the competent body to deal with them.

Brittan said: "I regard it as astonishing that we've been able to bring together such a diverse group of countiries and get agreement on a text that is not just papering over the cracks but genuinely important," he said.

He said he believed labour standards was a subject that should be discussed in the WTO and that cooperation between the WTO and the International Labour Organisation (ILO) was the right way to proceed.
"We have put our foot in the door on that," Brittan said.
He said that at the same time, developing countries had been assured that labour could not be used as a protectionist weapon and that cheap labour was not an unfair practise.
